reference.source: Williams Hematology / Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive bleeding disorder, most often from mutations in the F13A1 gene encoding the catalytic A subunit
Classic presentation is delayed bleeding after an initial clot forms, because the fibrin clot is unstable and breaks down
Umbilical stump bleeding in the neonatal period is a characteristic early clue
There is a high risk of intracranial haemorrhage, which makes lifelong prophylaxis important in severe deficiency
Impaired wound healing and recurrent pregnancy loss reflect the role of factor XIII in fibrin crosslinking and placental stability
Routine coagulation screens (prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, thrombin time) are normal, so the diagnosis is missed unless specifically sought
Diagnosis requires a specific factor XIII activity assay, and management uses factor XIII concentrate replacement including regular prophylaxis
reference.pathophysiology: Factor XIII is a transglutaminase that, once activated by thrombin, crosslinks fibrin monomers and incorporates antifibrinolytic proteins into the clot, converting a loose fibrin mesh into a mechanically strong, lysis-resistant structure. In congenital deficiency, usually due to biallelic mutations affecting the A subunit, the initial platelet plug and fibrin clot still form, so standard clotting times are normal, but the clot is not stabilised and disintegrates prematurely. This produces the hallmark of delayed bleeding after an interval of apparent haemostasis. Because factor XIII crosslinking also supports tissue repair and the maintenance of the placenta, its deficiency causes poor wound healing and recurrent miscarriage in addition to a bleeding tendency, and the loss of clot stability predisposes to spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage.
additionalDifferentials: Other rare inherited coagulation factor deficiencies
Alpha-2 antiplasmin or PAI-1 deficiency (other clot-stability defects)
Acquired factor XIII deficiency or inhibitors
Vitamin K deficiency or warfarin effect (excluded by normal screens)
additionalInvestigations: Specific factor XIII activity assay, the key diagnostic test
Standard coagulation screen (typically normal) to exclude other factor deficiencies
Clot solubility test as a historical qualitative screen where activity assays are unavailable
Factor XIII subunit antigen assays to distinguish A- from B-subunit deficiency
Genetic testing of F13A1 and F13B
Neuroimaging when intracranial haemorrhage is suspected
redFlags: Any suspicion of intracranial haemorrhage, which is a leading cause of death
Umbilical stump or delayed post-surgical bleeding in an undiagnosed patient
Recurrent pregnancy loss in a woman with a bleeding history
Poor or dehiscing wound healing suggesting defective clot stabilisation
reference.prognosis: With regular factor XIII concentrate prophylaxis the prognosis is generally good and life-threatening bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage, can be largely prevented, whereas untreated severe deficiency carries significant morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Excluding a bleeding disorder because routine coagulation screens are normal
Failing to consider the diagnosis in neonatal umbilical bleeding or delayed post-injury bleeding
Overlooking factor XIII replacement to support pregnancy in affected women
Not offering prophylaxis in severe deficiency given the intracranial haemorrhage risk
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Regular prophylaxis with factor XIII concentrate as the mainstay in severe deficiency, exploiting its long half-life for infrequent dosing
Cryoprecipitate or fresh frozen plasma for treatment or prophylaxis where concentrate is unavailable
On-demand factor XIII replacement for acute bleeding and surgical cover
Continuous factor XIII replacement throughout pregnancy to prevent miscarriage and support placental stability
Antifibrinolytics as an adjunct for mucosal bleeding
Neuroimaging and urgent replacement for suspected intracranial haemorrhage, with patient education about the characteristic delayed bleeding
Monitoring of trough factor XIII levels with haematology follow-up, and genetic counselling given autosomal recessive inheritance
